correspondences.rationale: Both denote a physical fibre break that prevents light from passing.
Both denote a sudden increase in fibre-span attenuation, such as from a bend or stressed cable.
Both denote disconnection of a patch lead or connector that interrupts the optical path.
Both denote connector contamination that introduces optical loss or degradation.
Both describe a hard amplifier or pump failure resulting in no optical output.
Both denote amplifier gain falling below its configured set point.
A rise in amplifier noise figure is the operator-model expression of excess amplifier-added optical noise.
Both denote non-flat amplifier gain across the optical band.
Both denote pump ageing evidenced by progressively increasing pump drive current.
Both denote a hardware failure of a coherent terminal's transmit laser.
Both denote a receiver-local degradation that adds a signal penalty.
Both denote transmit-laser ageing evidenced by upward bias-current drift.
Both denote slow erosion of an optical channel's reception margin.
Both denote frequency misalignment of a WSS or router passband for one channel.
Both denote failure of a WSS/router directional input port, blocking traffic entering through it.
Both denote an increase in differential group delay on the upstream optical path.
Both denote a rapid transient change in optical state of polarisation.
Both denote a hard failure of an OTN cross-connect's switching fabric.
Both denote a wrongly configured OTN cross-connect that delivers an ODU to the wrong destination.
Both denote a physical failure of the customer-facing client or tributary port or optic.
Both are deliberately nonspecific placeholders for a fault somewhere on the relevant end-to-end or upstream path.
Both denote absent light or power below the receiver's detection threshold.
Both denote an optical signal whose received power is too low.
Both denote loss of the optical supervisory channel on the immediately feeding span.
Both denote excessive optical noise or reduced OSNR.
Both describe a fast state-of-polarisation change; model A additionally states that it exceeds receiver tracking capability.
Both denote excessive differential group delay at the receiver.
Both denote quality degradation from spectral clipping, narrowing, or passband misalignment, potentially with normal power.
Both denote receiver-local degradation that does not propagate along the optical route.
Both denote an equipment-level unit failure that stops traffic and invalidates or stops monitoring.
Both denote loss of OTU frame alignment at a line receiver.
Both denote pre-FEC errors above the degradation threshold while frame alignment remains available.
Both denote an ODU Alarm Indication Signal propagating downstream and being present at an ODU receiver.
Both denote an ODU being delivered to the wrong destination by a cross-connect.
Both denote interruption of the client service carried by the affected tributary.
Both denote a brief client-service interruption caused by protection switching.
Both denote rising amplifier pump drive as the pump ages.
Both denote increasing transmit-laser bias caused by ageing.
Both denote a channel margin that declines gradually.
Both are total optical-power measurements at an amplifier input.
Both are total optical-power measurements at an amplifier output.
Both express current amplifier pump drive as a percentage of its commissioning or beginning-of-life baseline.
Both express transmitter laser bias as a percentage of its commissioning or beginning-of-life value.
Both denote optical power measured at a line receiver.
Both denote per-channel OSNR estimated by coherent receiver processing.
Both denote the received bit-error ratio measured before forward-error correction.
Both are coherent-receiver measurements of differential group delay.
Both measure the rate of change of the received state of polarisation.
Model A's counter explicitly includes customer errored seconds and gives a 15-minute reporting example, matching the client PM15 counter.
Both count seconds during which the client service is unavailable, conventionally in 15-minute performance bins.
Both denote the optical amplifier at the transmitting or launch end of an optical multiplex section.
Both denote an inline optical amplifier at an intermediate repeater site.
Both denote the receiving-end preamplifier immediately before the next routing or terminal stage.
Both denote a line interface mapping one client service onto one coherent wavelength.
Both denote a line interface aggregating several client services onto one wavelength.
Both denote an OTN line card interfacing a coherent line signal to digital ODU switching.
Both denote the WSS-based optical switching function that independently routes wavelengths among directions.
Both denote an OTN switch containing an ODU cross-connect fabric.
Both denote a customer-facing port that maps a client signal into an ODU.
Both denote every optical channel in the affected multiplexed signal.
Both denote one optical channel.
Both denote a proper subset of channels, particularly channels near one band edge.
Both denote every wavelength entering a ROADM or router through one directional input port.
Both scope a condition to the equipment unit itself rather than its traffic.
Both denote only the particular local receiver.
Both denote every ODU cross-connected through the affected switch or fabric.
Both denote a single ODU.
Both denote the particular client service under discussion.
Both identify the local equipment unit that raised the alarm or observed the change.
Both identify the local alarm-reporting port; model A specializes it to a customer tributary.
Both denote the fibre span immediately preceding and feeding the unit.
Both denote the amplifier immediately before the span that feeds the current unit.
Both denote the input patch connection at the head of the optical multiplex or wavelength section.
Both denote any upstream span, amplifier, section input, or router element on the signal path.
Both denote either endpoint client or tributary port of the service.
Both denote an OTN switch or cross-connect traversed by the service's ODU path.
The vendor's primary protected route is the operator model's working ODU path.
The vendor's standby route is the operator model's protection ODU path.
Both denote the ODU path currently carrying the service, whether working or protection.
Both denote the complete lightpath between the local unit and the far-end line interface, including the far endpoint.
Both denote standard monitoring supplied on every unit without an optional telemetry package.
Both denote the optional capability exposing optical input, output, and received-power measurements.
Both denote optional per-channel optical monitoring of channel power and OSNR.
Both denote advanced coherent-DSP and equipment-health telemetry, including OSNR, pre-FEC errors, DGD, polarisation, and drive currents.
Both denote an abrupt failure mode in which traffic or signal is lost.
Both denote reduced signal or service quality while traffic may continue.
Both denote a slowly developing trend that precedes eventual failure, though model B additionally specifies that traffic is not yet affected.
Both are the highest operational alarm priority for immediate service or equipment failure.
Both denote a significant alarm priority below the highest level.
Both denote a lower-priority warning for degradation, ageing, or reduced resilience.
Both represent informational condition reporting without an actionable alarm priority.
Both denote independent per-channel routing, with line-wide conditions continuing on each routed wavelength.
